national.title: Mississippi Senate race is toss-up, with razor-thin margin
national.summary: The Senate race in deep-red Mississippi remains unresolved Wednesday morning, as Democrat Scott Colom has mounted a surprisingly competitive challenge to incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.
national.body: Washington — The Senate midterm race in deep-red Mississippi remains unresolved, with Democrat Scott Colom mounting a surprisingly competitive challenge to incumbent GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. With about 96% of the vote in, at one point Wednesday morning just a few dozen votes separated the candidates, a stunningly close result in the Magnolia State. By early Thursday morning, Colom was leading Hyde-Smith by just over 1,100 votes. Hyde-Smith, 67, has been in the Senate since 2018 and is seeking reelection. But Colom, a district attorney, launched a formidable challenge, and could deliver Democrats yet another victory. Democrats saw a slew of wins in Senate races Tuesday night, including in states that President Trump won by double digits in the 2024 elections. With more than four flips of GOP-held seats, Democrats secured enough seats to take control of the chamber in the new year. If Colom manages to pull off a victory, he would add to their majority. Colom, 43, is a seventh-generation Mississippian who campaigned on cost of living and health care issues. Democrats began investing in the race in recent weeks, seeing an opportunity for a pickup. But the possible outcome still appeared exceedingly unlikely heading into Election Day.Mr. Trump won Mississippi by 20 points in 2024, and the state hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1982. Speaking to supporters in the wee hours of the morning on Wednesday, Colom said, "The results are all trending in our direction.""We are trending in counties that people thought we had no chance to compete in," Colom said. "And we're winning them."The unresolved race in Mississippi comes as Alaska's Senate race is also outstanding, leaving the size of Democrats' majority up in the air.

national.summary: Portugal legend Cristiano Ronaldo says he is retiring from international football.
national.body:
Portugal legend Cristiano Ronaldo says he is retiring from international football.

The 41-year-old forward has scored 146 goals and won 234 caps for his country - both world records - since making his debut in 2003.

He walked out of the Portugal camp in September after being told he would not start the Nations League match against Denmark.

"To the Portuguese people, the day has come for me to hand back the number seven shirt of our national team," Ronaldo said in an Instagram video. , external

"I never felt it belonged to me alone, but for 23 years I had the privilege and responsibility of wearing it, defending it and carrying it with me into stadiums all around the world.

"Today the time has come to pass it on to the future. It was not an easy decision, because some decisions are not made with the mind alone - they are also made with the heart.

"A journey that began in August 2003 and changed my life forever has come to an end."

On Friday Portugal will announce their squad for this month's Nations League fixtures - against Denmark at home and Wales away.

national.summary: Cristiano Ronaldo says he won't play for Portugal anymore, ending a career that spanned six World Cups and included a European title and the men's all-time international scoring record.
national.body: Lisbon, Portugal — Cristiano Ronaldo announced on Thursday he won't play for Portugal anymore, ending a career that spanned six World Cups and included a European title and the men's all-time international scoring record.The announcement marked the end of a lauded career that began more than two decades ago before Euro 2004 and finished with him walking out on the national team after a falling out with coach Jorge Jesus. "To the Portuguese people, the day has come for me to hand back the No. 7 shirt of our national team," the 41-year-old Ronaldo said in a long video message on social media. "I never felt it belonged to me alone but for 23 years I had the privilege and the responsibility of wearing it, defending it and carrying it with me into stadiums all around the world. "Today the time has come to pass it on to the future. It was not an easy decision because some decisions are not made with the mind alone. They are also made with the heart. A journey that began in August 2003 and changed my life forever has come to an end." While long-time peer Lionel Messi finished his career with Argentina after a much anticipated farewell match last month, Ronaldo's final appearance with Portugal has ended up being on Sept. 24 in a 1-0 win over Wales in the Nations League. Jesus kept him on the bench for the following match and said he didn't plan to start him in the next one, so Ronaldo decided to leave the team's training camp. Jesus later said Ronaldo would be welcome back and the decision to return was up to him. The Portuguese soccer federation released a statement expressing "deep gratitude and immense admiration" for Ronaldo's service to the country. "Cristiano Ronaldo has raised Portugal's profile and inspired generations of young people who dream of following in his footsteps; for many of us, he is the greatest player of all time!" the federation said. It said it intends to organize a tribute to Ronaldo "in which the fans and the country can one more time applaud and celebrate a player who has given us so much." Like Messi, Ronaldo will keep playing at club level, and is expected to finish his club career at the end of this season with Al-Nassr in Saudi Arabia. He is in pursuit of his 1,000th career goal and has 985. national.title: Was an Italian chef really fired over refusal to put pineapple on pizza?
national.summary: The chef had stated that putting pineapple on pizza was "offensive to his culture".
national.body:
Was an Italian chef really fired over refusal to put pineapple on pizza? Close Italian chef Davide Tamburella was fired from a Brisbane restaurant in May after the establishment's management expressed concerns about a string of complaints about the chef's behaviour.

Among them were Tamburella's refusal to provide ham and pineapple pizza for guests at a function.

It was the third time Tamburella had refused to use the fruit on pizzas in the past four years.

At the time, the chef had stated that putting pineapple on pizza was "offensive to his culture".

Australia correspondent Katy Watson explains what led to Tamburella's dismissal.

national.title: France gears up for strikes and protests as unions promise national mobilisation
national.summary: Five of France's unions have joined a wave of strikes and protests in a national day of action.
national.body:
Hundreds of thousands of demonstrators are expected to take part in marches across France as five unions join strikes and protests in a national day of action.

The protests began in September with high school students complaining about poor conditions and resources in education, but have spread to include the so-called "yellow-vest" movement and workers.

Authorities expect 500,000 to 700,000 demonstrators to join marches, with tens of thousands more in Paris alone, in a day billed by one union leader as "a great day of convergence".

The five unions have combined forces across the public and private sector, with demands for higher wages to combat the cost of living and protected public services.

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez has said that 70,000 police and gendarmes are being deployed, vowing "an extremely firm response" to any potential outbreaks of violence.

More than 250 separate actions are planned for 5 November, with some disruption reported in schools, hospitals and public transport.

Workers have also been asked to halt production at oil refineries, and France is expected to import more electricity than it produces on Thursday because of disruption at nuclear plants.

A coalition of unions has urged workers, pensioners and young people to join Thursday's day of strikes to intensify pressure on the government. In particular they are seeking a rise in the minimum wage, or Smic , which is currently €12.31 (£10) an hour.

national.title: Trump's arch is on the verge of federal approval. But a judge could block construction
national.summary: A federal panel will meet to consider the arch for final approval on Thursday, and the government said it may begin construction later that same day. Critics hope a judge will intervene last-minute.
national.body:
The government submitted final renderings to the National Capital Planning Commission that depict a 250-foot arch topped with three gold statues and an eternal flame. Department of the Interior hide caption

This could be a make-or-break week for President Trump's triumphal arch.

For months, the Trump administration has barreled toward his dream of building a 250-foot arch in Washington, D.C.: rubber-stamping and side-stepping various federal reviews, cutting out Congress and announcing imminent construction despite a lack of final approval and an ongoing legal battle.

In May, the entirely Trump-appointed Commission for Fine Arts approved the arch's design — still incomplete at the time . In September, a federal council packed with Trump allies abruptly terminated a historic preservation review that participants had already criticized as rushed .

Politics As Trump's proposed arch looms over D.C., protesters pin their hopes on the midterms It all comes to a head on Thursday, when the National Capital Planning Commission will meet to consider final approval for the controversial structure. The arch is the only item on the agenda; the meeting will be online-only and is expected to take five hours because of the high volume of public participation.

Nearly 120 concerned citizens have signed up to speak, an unusually high number for such meetings and a symbol of the widespread public opposition. Democratic lawmakers, veterans, historic preservationists and more than 100,000 people have spoken out against the arch in written comments, local protests and previous commission meetings.

Among their many concerns , critics say the structure would obstruct an important view , insult service members buried on the hallowed ground of nearby Arlington National Cemetery and add a layer of risk to notoriously complicated D.C. airspace. They see the arch as part of Trump's unilateral effort to memorialize himself in the nation's capital.

The White House has repeatedly said the arch will "enhance the visitor experience at Arlington National Cemetery" and be "one of the most iconic landmarks not only in Washington, D.C., but throughout the world."

national.title: As budgets tighten, people are breaking out their library cards
national.summary: Some Americans squeezed by high prices are relying more on their local libraries for things like books, streaming services and high-priced items like musical instruments and sewing machines.
national.body:
Izzy Rivera reads at least one book every week, but buying them new isn't in her budget. As she saves up for law school, some expenses don't make the cut.

"Say I'm buying a few a month," she said, "it just isn't realistic."

That's why Rivera has recently been leaning more on local libraries near her home in Topeka, Kan., checking out both physical books and digital copies on the Libby app. (Some of her recent reads: Sour Cherry by Natalia Theodoridou, Spoilt Creatures by Amy Twigg and Plastic Inc. by Beth Gardiner.) Rivera also went to her library's used book sale last month, where she picked up 15 books for about $20.

The library's money-saving potential doesn't end there for her. Rivera also watches movies on the streaming app Kanopy, reads the New York Times at no cost and often passes the time at a local branch.

Business This is how close American households are to the financial edge "It's somewhere I can go where I'm not expected to spend money," she said. "If I were to go to a coffee shop just to get out and do something, the expectation would be to buy a coffee, even though I probably didn't want a coffee."

It is something of a truism in the library world that, when economic conditions worsen, people use libraries more. Patrons and librarians across the U.S. tell NPR they're seeing that pan out now.

Prices for food and other everyday items continue to rise in part because of the war with Iran, and affordability was a top concern among voters heading into the midterm elections. According to a Pew Research Center survey released in mid-October, 44% of Americans say they've struggled in the past year to afford at least one basic necessity, such as medical care or their rent or mortgage payment. Seventy percent of adults also said they've cut back on "extras," such as subscriptions to streaming services.

Data shared with NPR by several of the largest public library systems in the U.S. show recent upticks in cardholder membership, circulation and event attendance. Librarians say part of that can be attributed to the rising cost of living — and the growing recognition that libraries' resources extend far beyond physical books.

national.title: Does the blue wave mean lower gasoline and diesel prices soon? Don't hold your breath
national.summary: A new Democratic majority in Congress could pressure the president to end the war in Iran. But it will be harder for them to directly affect fuel prices, which are tied to a complex international oil market.
national.body:
A customer replaces the nozzle on a gasoline pump after making a purchase at Fuel City filling station Friday, April 17, 2026, in Dallas. Tony Gutierrez/AP hide caption

Democrats are now poised to take control of Congress by wide margins — and a critical driver of their success has been voter fury about how the war in Iran has driven up the cost of fuel.

Before the war, about one fifth of the world's oil passed through the Strait of Hormuz. As the war throttled that waterway , the price of oil rose : A barrel of Brent crude cost about $70 in late February, spent months hovering around the $110 mark, and is now close to $95.

That's driven up the price of everything that's refined from crude. A gallon of gas costs $4.12 on average — about $1 higher than a year ago. The price of diesel hit a record high in September at $6.52, and while it's fallen a bit since then, a gallon remains about $2.50 higher than this time last year, according to AAA .

Business Oil company earnings skyrocket — again Business Tariffs, diesel and computer chips are driving up costs for automakers These soaring prices helped major oil companies rake in huge profits over the past two quarters , while making the cost of fuel at the pump uncomfortably high for drivers, and boosting the price of nearly everything in a nation that is heavily reliant on trucking .

So now that the midterm results are in, could drivers see lower gasoline and diesel prices anytime soon?

Nothing yet — members of the new Congress won't be sworn in until January.

Middle East conflict Why it's so hard for world leaders to bring down oil and gasoline prices Business Why Trump just loosened the rules on 'dyed diesel' — normally a farm fuel And once they are seated, U.S. legislators have limited powers to directly affect the price of oil, which is dictated by a complex global market.

national.title: The South flexes political power in midterms, sets regional influence in 2028 election
national.summary: Tuesday's dramatic midterm results have transformed the electoral map, ensuring the path to future power for Democrats and Republicans must run through the South and its diverse voting population.
national.body:
Tuesday's dramatic midterm results have transformed the electoral map, ensuring the future path to power for Democrats and Republicans alike must run through the South.

Black voter turnout surged in states like Louisiana and Georgia, as Democrats flipped Senate seats in North Carolina, South Carolina and Texas. Mississippi is too close to call.

Republican-led efforts to redraw House districts to gain more favorable districts in places like Alabama, North Carolina, Texas and Florida backfired, with Democrats poised to net several seats in the region.

In several states, the margins at the top of the ticket were so large that the blue tsunami carried down ballot races along with it, flipping several state legislative chambers and statewide offices along the way.

Even in contests where Democrats ultimately did not prevail, the millions of dollars of investment from both sides and the wide-ranging repudiation of the Trump administration from every demographic group highlight the South's important role in control of Congress and the White House in future election cycles.

In the aftermath of a Supreme Court ruling earlier this year that gutted part of the Voting Rights Act, Republican-led Southern states rushed to redraw House maps to create additional seats that would better withstand a midterm environment where voters punished the party in power.

They included changes in Tennessee that split Memphis into three districts (and where Democratic state Rep. Justin Pearson is within a few thousand votes of winning), a redraw of several Alabama districts that sought to unseat Rep. Shomari Figures (who won by nearly 8 points in the new Trump +14 configuration) and a target of nine seats in Texas and Florida.

As of Wednesday night, Republicans have won one of them, according to a race call by the Associated Press.

Tuesday's dramatic midterm results have transformed the electoral map, ensuring the future path to power for Democrats and Republicans alike must run through the South.

Black voter turnout surged in states like Louisiana and Georgia, as Democrats flipped Senate seats in North Carolina, South Carolina and Texas. Mississippi is too close to call.

Republican-led efforts to redraw House districts to gain more favorable districts in places like Alabama, North Carolina, Texas and Florida backfired, with Democrats poised to net several seats in the region.

In several states, the margins at the top of the ticket were so large that the blue tsunami carried down ballot races along with it, flipping several state legislative chambers and statewide offices along the way.

Even in contests where Democrats ultimately did not prevail, the millions of dollars of investment from both sides and the wide-ranging repudiation of the Trump administration from every demographic group highlight the South's important role in control of Congress and the White House in future election cycles.

In the aftermath of a Supreme Court ruling earlier this year that gutted part of the Voting Rights Act, Republican-led Southern states rushed to redraw House maps to create additional seats that would better withstand a midterm environment where voters punished the party in power.

They included changes in Tennessee that split Memphis into three districts (and where Democratic state Rep. Justin Pearson is within a few thousand votes of winning), a redraw of several Alabama districts that sought to unseat Rep. Shomari Figures (who won by nearly 8 points in the new Trump +14 configuration) and a target of nine seats in Texas and Florida.

As of Wednesday night, Republicans have won one of them, according to a race call by the Associated Press.

national.body: An Indiana man who admitted killing his girlfriend's two children was executed early Thursday in the first of three lethal injections scheduled for the same day in the U.S. Jeffrey Weisheit killed the children, ages 8 and 5, by setting fire to his girlfriend's house in the Evansville area in 2010. Weisheit died at the Indiana State Prison in Michigan City. The lethal injection started just after midnight and he was pronounced dead at 12:45 a.m., according to Noelle Russell, Indiana Department of Correction chief communications officer. She said Weisheit's final meal was barbecue ribs and he had no final words. Florida and Alabama were also set to carry out executions Thursday, which would mark the second time this year that three people in the U.S. would be put to death on the same day.Alabama, Tennessee and Oklahoma conducted executions on Aug. 13. It would be Florida's 19th execution this year under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, matching a record set by the state in 2025, but was the first this year in Indiana. The death penalty has faced renewed scrutiny following the September failed execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee, although courts have rejected efforts to halt other executions since she survived two lethal doses of pentobarbital.Pike said in a statement dictated to her lawyers and released a month after the botched execution that she's been in pain every moment since she woke up confused in a hospital. "I had not contemplated life beyond that night," she said. Lawyers wanted Indiana Republican Gov. Mike Braun to allow Weisheit, 50, to undergo brain scans in an effort to reinforce their argument that he has a history of head injuries and mental health problems. Braun declined, and he also turned down a request to reduce the sentence to life in prison. Weisheit's latest objection centered on the state's planned use of lethal drugs purchased from a pharmacy that is facing a disciplinary hearing next week at the Indiana Pharmacy Board. The Indiana Department of Correction said it's confident "in our ability to humanely carry out" the execution. national.title: India's costliest film retells a beloved Hindu epic - but divides critics
national.summary: Easily the most anticipated Bollywood film of the year, Ramayana: Rise of a Legend is the first of two parts.
national.body:
India's most expensive film - a lavish retelling of the Hindu epic Ramayana, made in two parts for a reported $500m (£370m) - has opened in cinemas worldwide, sparking enormous expectations and mixed reviews.

Directed by Nitesh Tiwari, Ramayana: Rise of a Legend is the first of two planned films, a sprawling production that brings together some of India's biggest stars, Hollywood visual-effects expertise and two Oscar-winning composers in an attempt to take one of the country's most revered stories to a global audience.

One of Hinduism's foundational epics, the Ramayana has travelled across centuries and continents, finding expression in poetry, temple sculpture, shadow puppetry, folk theatre and stories passed down through generations. It has outlasted kingdoms and empires, inspired religious devotion and political movements, and found new life, again and again, on TV and in cinema.

Tiwari's version returns to the familiar story of love, duty, exile and war, set in a world of gods and demons, celestial weapons and mighty kingdoms.

Ranbir Kapoor plays Lord Ram, the virtuous prince of Ayodhya. Banished from his kingdom for 14 years, he retreats to the forest with his wife Sita (played by Sai Pallavi), who is kidnapped by Ravana, the 10-headed king of Lanka.

Played by Yash, one of southern India's biggest stars, Ravana is a powerful warrior whose pride leads him into an epic battle with Ram (which will be depicted in part 2, set to release next year).

The film's producer, Namit Malhotra, heads visual-effects company DNEG , which has worked on Hollywood blockbusters including Dune and Interstellar. The music is a collaboration between AR Rahman, the Oscar-winning Indian composer of Slumdog Millionaire, and Hans Zimmer, whose scores for Gladiator, The Dark Knight and Dune have helped define the sound of modern Hollywood.

The film opened days ahead of Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights which celebrates Ram's return to Ayodhya after his exile.

national.title: Joshua Wong, face of Hong Kong's pro-democracy protests, jailed for 10 years
national.summary: Wong, 30, is among hundreds of Hongkongers detained under the controversial national security law.
national.body:
Joshua Wong, once the face of Hong Kong's democracy movement, has been sentenced to 10 years in jail for colluding with foreign forces under the city's sweeping national security law.

Wong is among hundreds of campaigners and ordinary Hongkongers arrested under the law, which was imposed in 2020 following explosive pro-democracy protests against Beijing's growing control.

Critics say the far-reaching law has silenced dissent, but authorities argue that it is needed to maintain stability and deny it has weakened the city's cherished autonomy.

Having already spent the last six years in jail, Wong, who was due to be freed in January, will now spend another decade behind bars.

Pope Leo XIV, left, and the singer and Nobel prize winner Bob Dylan, right, pose for a photo during a meeting in the Vatican on Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026. Vatican Media/LaPresse/via AP hide caption

VATICAN CITY — Bob Dylan came knockin' on Pope Leo XIV' s door Wednesday, as the American singer-songwriter and poet visited with the American pope at the Vatican during a break between concert dates in Italy.

The Vatican said the encounter was brief, with Leo giving Dylan a rosary and Dylan presenting the pope with a copy of his autobiography, "Chronicles: Volume One."

Book Reviews 'After the Flood' argues Bob Dylan's late career is just as potent as his early years Leo had quoted from an unpublished protest song Dylan penned in 1963, "Go Away You Bomb," in his 2026 book "Disarmed and Disarming: Peace Is a Gift."

Leo was warning against the race to rearm and the recourse to nuclear weapons and quoted the lyric, addressed to a hypothetical atomic bomb: "I hate you cause yer man-made and man-owned, an' man-handled."

Two Vatican officials accompanied Dylan: the Rev. Antonio Spadaro, a Vatican culture ministry official who also accompanied Patti Smith to a July audience with Leo; and Andrea Monda, the editor of the Vatican newspaper, L'Osservatore Romano.

Pope Leo XIV, right, and the singer and Nobel prize winner Bob Dylan, left, talk during a meeting in the Vatican on Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026. Vatican Media/LaPresse/via AP hide caption

Spadaro said Dylan had wanted to speak with Leo, and the two met in private for a few minutes. In an essay in L'Osservatore Romano, he recalled that the former Robert Prevost, who was born in Chicago in 1955, grew up familiar with Dylan's music.

national.body: Republicans undertook a historic effort to redraw several states' Congressional districts mid-decade in an attempt to maintain control of the House. That effort was rebuffed on Tuesday night as the GOP was on track to lose all of the districts it tried to gerrymander. There were several reasons that states undertook what had previously been a rare practice of mid-decade redistricting. Republican efforts started when President Trump ordered Texas lawmakers to redraw their map to net up to five seats for the GOP. But despite the all-out effort, Democrats won control of the House on Tuesday, with CBS News estimating Democrats could end up with 251 to 268 House seats. With the House decisively swinging toward Democrats and Democrats undertaking measures in a few states to counter the GOP's efforts, Republicans are faced with the possibility of having created a so-called "dummymander," a situation in which a party tries to gerrymander, but ends up benefiting the other party. national.title: Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong sentenced to 10 years in prison
national.summary: Wong was sentenced for his second conviction under a Beijing-imposed national security law, in a case that critics say reflects the crackdown on the city's once-thriving pro-democracy movement.
national.body:
FILE - Hong Kong teenage student leader Joshua Wong, left, stands in front of yellow umbrellas outside a magistrates' court in Hong Kong, on Sept. 2, 2015. Vincent Yu/AP hide caption

HONG KONG — Prominent Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong was sentenced to 10 years in prison Thursday for his second conviction under a Beijing-imposed national security law, in a case that critics say reflects the crackdown on the city's once-thriving pro-democracy movement.

Wong was charged in 2025 with conspiracy to collude with foreign forces to endanger national security under the law. In September, he pleaded guilty to the offense, a move that can typically reduce the sentence.

The 30-year-old is already serving a four-year, eight-month prison term for the city's biggest national security case linked to an unofficial primary after entering a guilty plea in that case. Before being prosecuted for the collusion-related charge, Wong had been expected to be freed in January 2027.

Judge William Tam said during the sentencing hearing that Wong's offense was of a grave nature and rejected that his role was limited.

He also said he considered a 13-year prison sentence as a starting point but reduced it because of Wong's guilty plea.

Wong looked calm and thanked his supporters before leaving the court. His supporters waved to him and Tiffany Chin, a former member of the now-disbanded Scholarism, once led by Wong, was in tears.

The judge said Wong could serve his two prison sentences concurrently. Wong only has about two months left on the sentence for his previous national security conviction.

national.title: Vance walks Trump tightrope with scathing election critique blaming Iran war
national.summary: The vice-president's blunt assessment of Republican election defeat marked one of the sharpest breaks with a sitting president in recent memory.
national.body:
Washington correspondent Published 5 November 2026, 02:33 GMT Updated 8 hours ago Vice-President JD Vance sent shockwaves through Washington on Wednesday by blaming his party's midterm defeat squarely on the Iran war, in what was widely interpreted as an effort to distance himself from President Donald Trump ahead of a potential 2028 White House run.

In a carefully calibrated, 600-word statement on X, the vice-president acknowledged that Trump's 2024 voters had deserted Republicans in the midterm election .

"The reason we lost is the war," he wrote. "The president himself said so last night."

In interviews late Tuesday night and Wednesday, Trump had defended the war but acknowledged that it played a factor in Democrats flipping control of the US House of Representatives and the Senate .

Vance's view on the war in Iran is an open secret in Washington. While he has repeatedly backed the conflict since the US and Israel attacked Tehran in February, he has reportedly expressed opposition in private meetings with administration officials.

But those disagreements had been kept out of the public eye - until now.

Hours after Trump and the party were handed a bruising election defeat, Vance made clear that he felt the decision to go to war was a clear political mistake.

"If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest," Vance said.

national.title: 2 Native American women make history in midterms
national.summary: In New Mexico, former Interior Secretary Deb Haaland was elected governor, making her the first Native American woman elected to lead a U.S. state. In Minnesota, Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan became the first Native American woman senator.
national.body: Two Native American women made history Tuesday night in the 2026 midterm elections, winning a Senate seat and a governorship — both firsts for Native women — as Democrats swept races across the country.In New Mexico, former Interior Secretary Deb Haaland was elected governor, making her the first Native American woman elected to lead a U.S. state. In Minnesota, Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan became the first Native American woman senator.Haaland, a citizen of Laguna Pueblo, was already the first Native American to serve as a Cabinet secretary. She defeated Republican Gregg Hull, former mayor of Rio Rancho, in the race for governor. Flanagan, an enrolled member of White Earth Nation, defeated Republican Michele Tafoya, a former sports broadcaster and conservative commentator. Who are they?Haaland has notched many firsts. She became the first Native American woman to chair a state political party in 2015 when she was elected to lead the Democratic Party of New Mexico. In 2018, she became one of the first two Native American women elected to Congress, alongside Rep. Sharice Davids of Kansas, who was reelected Tuesday. Haaland later served as former President Joe Biden's Interior secretary from 2021 until January 2025.On the trail, she spoke about raising her daughter alone, selling homemade salsa and relying at times on food stamps. "My story is a lot like many New Mexicans — humble beginnings," she told a Rio Rancho congregation in October.Flanagan got her start as an organizer, then served on the Minneapolis School Board and led the Children's Defense Fund Minnesota. She was elected to the Minnesota House of Representatives in 2015 and has been lieutenant governor since 2019, where she has helped reshape Minnesota's relationship with the state's 11 tribal nations. Raised by a single mother in Section 8 housing, Flanagan had childhood asthma that kept her in and out of hospitals. She's been an outspoken supporter of Medicaid, saying that it "saved [her] life." What do they stand for?Haaland ran on the cost of living, protecting New Mexico's Universal Child Care program and overhauling its child welfare system. local.title: When will we know the mayoral results in Fairport?
local.summary: Elections officials expect the bulk of the vote count to happen late next week.
local.body:
Elections officials don't expect to get into the thick of counting the more than 1,300 write-in ballots cast in the village of Fairport mayoral election until late next week.

Unofficial results show write-ins outnumber ballots cast for Democratic candidate Heidi Woika, currently the village’s deputy mayor. A bipartisan team will assess how many of those are for Tracy Briggs, a town trustee who lost the Democratic primary then waged an aggressive write-in campaign.

As it stood Wednesday, 95% of the recorded write-ins would need to be for Briggs for her to claim victory. Mail-in and affidavit ballots still are being processed, so vote tallies could change.

"I think people really know me as a person, and they've seen me out there doing the work, and I truly listen to them," Briggs said. "I never lost focus of why I got elected in the first place, and it really is to listen to the residents, to be their advocate and to be their liaison with their local government."

Elsewhere, the Chili town supervisor race also remains too close to call. Incumbent David Dunning, a Republican, leads Democratic challenger Emily Kalouch by less than 1 percentage point. No decision has been made on whether a recount will be necessary as that margin, too, could change with mail-in and affidavit ballots,

local.title: Blue wave misses area; Borrello, Molitor re-elected
local.summary: The blue wave that flipped offices from red to blue on Election Day is costing Republicans in the New York state Legislature as well. Statewide, it appears Democrats have reimagined their supermajorities in both the state Senate and state Assembly after flipping at least a dozen seats, including fiv
local.body:
The blue wave that flipped offices from red to blue on Election Day is costing Republicans in the New York state Legislature as well.

Statewide, it appears Democrats have reimagined their supermajorities in both the state Senate and state Assembly after flipping at least a dozen seats, including five on Long Island. Long Island's 31-member legislative delegation will remain largely Republican, but Democrats won enough seats there to extend their legislative majorities. The supermajority means Democrats can override a veto by Gov. Kathy Hochul, though the threatened override hasn't come into play often in the past.

“This achievement reflects the strength of our diverse coalition, representing communities from our largest cities to our smallest towns, and our shared commitment to moving New York forward," Senate Majority Leader Andrea Stewart-Cousins, D-Yonkers, said in a statement shortly before midnight on Tuesday.

Locally, the blue wave didn't affect state Sen. George Borrello or Assemblyman Andrew Molitor. The Republicans retained their seats, with Molitor winning re-election. With all districts reporting, Molitor received 26,485 votes while challenger Thomas A. Carle received 15,490 votes. Borrello won Chautauqua County’s vote for the 57th Senate District, 28,037-14,502 over challenger Victoria Guite-Williams. With all but one election district reporting across the 57th Senate District Borrello received 78,049 votes (68.04%) to Guite-Williams’ 33,922 votes (29.57%).

"I am humbled and grateful to the people of the 57th District for once again electing me to be their voice in Albany," Borrello said in a statement. "Over the past six years, I’ve worked hard to build a record that reflects the priorities of the people I represent. That means standing up for taxpayers, fighting for our farmers and small businesses, challenging costly energy mandates and working to keep our communities safe. I’ve never been afraid to speak out or take on a difficult fight when the well-being of the people I represent is at stake. The concerns I’ve heard from residents about affordability, energy policy, public safety and other key issues will continue to drive my work in Albany. We’ve made progress on some important issues, but there’s much more to do. I’ll keep fighting for policies that will reverse the decline we've experienced under one-party rule and the outmigration that has resulted. New York has so many assets and potential. With the right policies, we can be the Empire State again."

local.summary: PORTLAND — As Portland Supervisor Rich Lewis said at a recent Brocton Village Board meeting, “Code Enforcement is going through some changes.” Moving forward, the town of Portland and the village of Brocton will rely on Roger Britz Jr. as a part-time Code Enforcement Officer. local.body:
PORTLAND -- As Portland Supervisor Rich Lewis said at a recent Brocton Village Board meeting, "Code Enforcement is going through some changes."

Moving forward, the town of Portland and the village of Brocton will rely on Roger Britz Jr. as a part-time Code Enforcement Officer. Britz, of Fredonia, will work up to 20 hours per week over the course of the year. His hours will fluctuate depending on need.

There will also be a full-time Code Clerk dedicated to the clerical duties of the Code Enforcement Office. That position is open and will be filled in the near future. In the meantime, the town of Portland is relying on part-time clerical support.

"We are looking to have someone hired as soon as possible for that," Lewis said.

Britz fills a void left by Joshua Dobbs, who is no longer employed by the town of Portland. Dobbs was initially hired in March as a town-wide provisional Inspection Officer to serve both the town of Portland and the village of Brocton. Dobbs was recently out on medical leave, with former Code Enforcement Officer Wendy Spinuzza helping the two municipalities with code-related matters in the interim on an hourly basis.

The changes were made "after careful assessment and talk with Mayor (Craig) Miller", Lewis said. The shift will make the Code Enforcement Office more accessible for residents, Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. each week. Britz was appointed to the role on Oct. 14, and since then, Lewis said "he has made major strides." Britz has worked closely with Spinuzza as he gets up to speed in the new role.

"I think it's going to work out much better than what we've had in recent times," Lewis said.

One of the most notable properties in the village of Brocton that does not comply with the village code is 98 Old Mill Road, where a home was destroyed in a fatal fire on Christmas morning of 2024. The property has yet to be cleaned up.

local.body:
Rep. Nick Langworthy will remain the 23rd Congressional representative in Congress, though he will be taking on a different role in the House minority when the new Congress is seated in January.

Langworthy defeated Aaron Gies of Olean, 59.4% to 39.15%, with Langworthy receiving 181,807 of the 305,882 ballots cast. Langworthy won each county in the district, 68.19% to 29.85% in Allegany County, 64.8% to 33.75% in Cattaraugus County, 58.35% to 40.34% in Chemung County, 56.72% to 41.87% in Erie County, 58.82% to 39.52% in Niagara County, 65.15% to 33.65% in Schuyler County, 63.76% to 35.03% in Steuben County and 58.23% to 40.37% in Tioga County. The most ballots in the race were cast in Erie County (130,320) and Chautauqua County (43,293).

"Last night's election results are a win for common sense and the truth. The people of Western New York and the Southern Tier sent a loud and clear message that they know I fight for them in Washington. The results are a powerful affirmation of my record of putting more money in taxpayers' pockets, making our communities safer, strengthening rural healthcare, and protecting their access to affordable, reliable energy," Langworthy said early Wednesday morning. "This is where I was born and raised, and where I am raising my own family. The people of this district are why I fight–for a better future for them, their children, and their grandchildren. While we are forgotten by Albany, I will always make sure our region has a seat at the table in Washington."

Results in the 23rd District race indicate Republicans in Chautauqua County may not have turned out in as great a number as they did in 2024. Gies received 17,129 votes in Chautauqua County, slightly fewer votes than the 17,491 votes Tom Carle received when challenging Langworthy two years ago. That’s a decrease of roughly 2.1% from 2024 to 2026. Langworthy received 25,564 votes in Chautauqua County and 36,798 in 2024, a 30.5% decrease from two years ago.

The House of Representatives that Langworthy has been re-elected to will have a much different look.

Democrats have won control of Congress in Tuesday's 2026 midterm elections. Democrats flipped at least seven Senate seats in red states and battlegrounds alike: Kansas, which hasn't elected a Democratic senator in nearly a century, Iowa, Texas, Ohio, Maine, North Carolina and South Carolina. They held on to battleground seats in Georgia and Michigan. In the House, Democrats flipped more than two dozen districts, some that voted for Trump by double digits in 2024.

local.title: The OBSERVER’s View: Hochul needs to quit delaying on Kyra’s Law
local.summary: We’ve reached the time of year when Gov. Kathy Hochul begins signing legislation passed by the state Legislature before the end of its session in June. It’s ludicrous to us that this process takes half a year in some cases, particularly when it comes to legislation that was approved with overwhelmin
local.body:
We’ve reached the time of year when Gov. Kathy Hochul begins signing legislation passed by the state Legislature before the end of its session in June.

It’s ludicrous to us that this process takes half a year in some cases, particularly when it comes to legislation that was approved with overwhelming legislative support like Kyra’s Law (A.6194-C/S.5998). Kyra's Law is named in memory of 2-year-old Kyra Franchettie, who was shot and killed by her father during a court-ordered unsupervised visit in 2016, and was passed with bipartisan support in the state Legislature this year. It remains unsigned four months after the end of the legislative session and was raised by several local women who spoke with The Post-Journal on their experiences dealing with the aftermath of domestic violence. Kyra’s Law doesn’t just help women, though. There are cases in which men who have been awarded custody of their children deal with many of the same issues that the sponsors of Kyra’s Law are trying to deal with.

Kyra’s Law isn’t a cure-all for domestic violence, but two of the women who spoke with The Post-Journal and OBSERVER said it would likely help make their situations better. Kyra’s Law would require courts to conduct a review in custody and visitation proceedings involving allegations of domestic violence, child abuse or substantial risks of harm to a child warranting the court’s immediate attention. It would expand the evidence a court considers to include risk factors, such as threats to harm or kill, stalking, violence during pregnancy, unlawful dissemination of intimate images, coercive control and a recent pattern of substance abuse, It would also permit review of certain uncertified records in proceedings for temporary visitation and custody; allow waiver of notice in emergency ex parte applications; and make substantial risk findings a significant factor in custody and visitation determinations. Kyra's Law would also expand custody and visitation procedures in state Supreme Court by requiring courts to advise parties of counsel rights; require courts to explain on the record the basis for custody and visitation determinations; prohibit adverse inferences against protective parents or assumptions regarding a child’s reluctance to interact with a parent; and require recurring judicial training on child safety and domestic violence’ issues.

"I can honestly say after being through all of this, the worst agony is watching your child suffer and nobody can help," said one of the women. "I literally felt like I could die. That is the worst agony to ever go through; the emotional abuse and fear is worse than the physical. It affects your whole life. They're not connecting how detrimental this is to children and mothers, what these criminals are doing."

local.body:
For me, communications in 2026 boil down to telephone, texting, or email. I don't do smoke signals anymore.

Alas, my arthritic hands have consigned hand-written notes to the back burner. When I hand write, maybe the first line or two have some resemblance to my once clear penmanship. Then the fingers cramp, the wrist stops pushing, and the script becomes a scrawl rapidly descending towards chicken scratch. Sort of like a doctor's prescription.

So, with my handwriting on the fritz, the computer has become my favorite. I still like to send a handwritten personal greeting. But if it extends past two handwritten lines, the remainder is a printout, folded and inserted with the card or note. I write the envelope at a different time so it's legible enough for the post office's machine readers.

My computer is my lifeline. Because of this column and a bunch of other writerly commitments, I'm on my laptop first thing in the morning and last thing at night. My knotty, knobby fingers much prefer the keyboard to texting. The text letters and numbers on my phone are too tiny for my stiff joints - I only text as a last resort. Then just last week, I learned to hate my phones. Plural.

Yes, we still have a land line. We are probably one of the three or four families left in Warren who are still paying two phone bills. No, it's not because we have money to burn. It's because without the land line, we wouldn't have a way to find our cell phones!

The insurance people who sell Medicare programs have been constantly calling since the middle of October. They have until the first week in December to convince me - and oodles of other seniors – that we should change our insurance to their plan. I don't know how many insurers are out there trying to change my mind, but if I judge it by the telephone traffic, it's hundreds. They start promptly at 9:00 a.m. every weekday. At first, I was simply frustrated by the frequency. I listened to a few to get the gist of things. When I say "Hello," there is the telltale pause. Then a voice says hello... with an uplifted question mark at the end of the word. So of course, that's when I repeat our hello, which kicks on the recorded sales statement.

"Hello, this is Naomi. We have been trying to reach you for a week ...." Or, "This is Jennifer responding to your call for more insurance information...." No, I did not inquire about your insurance. And yes, if you've been trying for a week, it's because I don't want to talk to you. Leave me alone. PU-LEEZ. The number of these calls is ridiculously out of hand. It took me until this week to find the BLOCK button on the bottom of my landline receiver.

local.title: Senator’s remarks send scary message
local.summary: In the incredible amount of midterm elections news, there were totalitarian sounding words of Ellissa Slotkin, Democratic senator from Michigan. Her comments were a clear threat to make the lives of young people who aspired to and took jobs in the President Donald Trump administration miserable, wer
local.body:
In the incredible amount of midterm elections news, there were totalitarian sounding words of Ellissa Slotkin, Democratic senator from Michigan. Her comments were a clear threat to make the lives of young people who aspired to and took jobs in the President Donald Trump administration miserable, were but a momentary blip in the 24-hour news cycle.

However, what she said and the manner in which she spoke was both revealing and frightening since Democrats either knowingly or unknowingly very often fall into the psychological defense mechanism called "projection" which involves accusing someone else of a behavior or activity that you are already up to.

To begin, who is Slotkin? Until very recently, while I had heard the name, I have paid no attention to her career. Upon investigation, I found she is a learned woman with a bachelor's degree from Cornell and a Masters of International Affairs from Columbia University. In addition, she is fluent in both Arabic and Swahili. Following 9/11 she was recruited by the Central Intelligence Agency as a Middle East Analyst and served three tours in Iraq over a period of five years.

Following that she served on the National Security Council during the George W. Bush Administration and was asked to stay on during the President Barack Obama Administration. She later served in senior leadership roles at the Department of Defense, eventually serving as the Acting Assistant Secretary of Defense for International Affairs. Until 2019 Slotkin had mostly been known as the daughter of Curt Slotkin the inventor of the famous "Ballpark Frank" the kind that ” plump when you cook ’em.” But in 2018 Slotkin ran for and won election to the House of Representees, serving from 2019 until 2025 and then won a highly competitive race for the Senate defeating Rep. Mike Rogers.

During her political career, Slotkin has been controversial but after remarks made at a political forum at the University of Chicago on Oct. 13, she rose to new heights of controversial speech. She advocated pursuing what she called "signature cases" involving President Trump and those around him. She said, "I want to look at these signature cases not focusing on the president but on the people who enabled him. Continuing, she said that she wanted young people considering jobs in the Trump administration to worry that doing so "might be buying myself a ton of problems that I don't want. I want that deterrence message sent"

local.title: Blue Devils qualify for first SUNYAC final in program history
local.summary: PLATTSBURGH – Haley Drinon and Avery Aloi scored goals and goalkeeper Alyssa Hatch finished with a shutout as the Fredonia State women’s soccer team advanced to its first SUNYAC Tournament final in program history on Wednesday afternoon by defeating Plattsburgh State 2-0 in the semifinals at the Fie
local.body:
PLATTSBURGH - Haley Drinon and Avery Aloi scored goals and goalkeeper Alyssa Hatch finished with a shutout as the Fredonia State women’s soccer team advanced to its first SUNYAC Tournament final in program history on Wednesday afternoon by defeating Plattsburgh State 2-0 in the semifinals at the Field House Complex.

The Blue Devils, who will play in the championship game Saturday against Cortland, wasted little time getting on the board. In the ninth minute, Drinon found the back of the net to give Fredonia a 1-0 advantage just 8:14 into the contest. Fredonia continued to pressure throughout the opening half, holding a 9-6 edge in shots and a commanding 7-3 advantage in corner kicks before taking the one-goal lead into halftime.

Fredonia State gained breathing room in the 71st minute when Aloi scored her second goal of the season, extending the lead to two goals. The Devils (12-3-4) then closed out the final 20 minutes to preserve the shutout and touch off celebration as the final whistle confirmed a historic victory.

“It’s an incredible feeling to see our team rewarded for all their efforts and their dedication to what it takes to be a student-athlete,” head coach Chris Case said. “The group is having fun and is hitting all cylinders at the right time. We had an outstanding effort from our group today. They competed for each other and it showed.”

Hatch totaled three saves in goal as Fredonia State snapped an 11-game winless streak against Plattsburgh (0-9-2 record). Last year’s campaign ended on the same stage and at the same location: a semifinal loss at Plattsburgh. The Blue Devils’ last win over the Cardinals occurred in 2014.

“We had an outstanding effort from our entire group today. They competed for each other and it showed,” Case said. “We beat a very good Plattsburgh team on the road at a very difficult place to play. It’s extra special for us to find success after losing this same game a year ago to them to end our season. Alyssa Hatch made some big, key saves for us. She played her best game in a Fredonia uniform.”

Cortland -- Fredonia's opponent on Saturday -- earned a berth in the title game by virtue of a 3-1 win over Oswego State yesterday.

local.body: First responders who went above and beyond to save lives were recognized Wednesday night during Mercy Hospital’s annual EMS Awards Dinner.The event honored emergency medical crews whose quick actions made a difference during life-threatening emergencies, including the rescue of a 34-year-old man found face down in a backyard.For Skip Yuhnke, a paramedic with the Elma Fire Department, the call was a reminder of why he has dedicated nearly five decades to emergency medical services.“I got a monitor on him and I gave him one shock, but it took a lot more than that to get him to come around and get pulses and to start breathing again,” Yuhnke said.Despite his years of experience, Yuhnke said successfully bringing someone back after cardiac arrest is rare, making calls like this especially meaningful.“When you get somebody that comes back and you can actually save them, or you make their life better, or you help them so they do have a better outcome in their life, that's what it's all about to me,” he said.Next year, Yuhnke will mark 50 years as an EMT.Kenneth Peterson, deputy fire commissioner for EMS with Buffalo Fire, said the awards dinner recognizes the dedication of first responders who put their communities first.“They are individuals that come from all walks of life that choose to both volunteer, compensated, to wake up in the middle of the night at a moment's notice and respond to calls for service, typically medical in nature,” Peterson said.Peterson said the dinner is also an opportunity to recognize those who often put their own busy lives aside to help others.Elizabeth Forkel with Erie County MERS said first responders do not always receive the recognition they deserve, despite the long hours and sacrifices they make.“A lot of first responders go unrecognized for their work. They work day in, day out, long hours, sometimes for free,” Forkel said. “A lot of times they're volunteer agencies, and this really goes to show just how important they are to the community.”WATCH: Mercy Hospital honors first responders for life-saving effortsFor Yuhnke, the recognition is meaningful, but the greatest reward is knowing he helped give someone another chance at life."It means a whole lot, because I've been doing this for almost 50 years. local.summary: While Democrats saw a historic election night, Republicans like Nick Langworthy retained their seats. Now, both sides are reflecting on the local race and national implications moving forward.
local.body: While Democrats saw a historic election night, Republicans like Nick Langworthy retained their seats for another term. Now, both sides are reflecting on the local race and the national implications moving forward.Langworthy won reelection for New York’s 23rd Congressional District against Democratic challenger Aaron Gies. Langworthy was first elected to Congress in 2022 and previously served as chairman of the New York State Republican Committee.With 97% of the votes reported, Langworthy secured 60.26% of the vote, over Gies' 39.69%. However, while the RepublicaN incumbent’s victory was still by a large percentage of the vote, Gies was able to chip away 26,500 votes from Langworthy's 2022 re-election bid."We cut Nick Langworthy's margin way down. And we showed folks that there is a better way to do things, and I'm proud of that," Aaron Gies told WKBW on Wednesday. "It was obviously disappointing to lose our race, but last night was a party because of the overwhelming result nationwide."Democrats secured control of the Senate after pulling off surprise victories in traditionally Republican strongholds, including Texas and Kansas. local.title: 'She loved helping people': Family remembers nurse killed while riding bicycle
local.summary: The family of a 43-year nursing veteran who died after being struck by a car while riding her bicycle in Cheektowaga is remembering her dedication to her family, her patients and her passion for cycling.
local.body: The family of a 43-year nursing veteran who died after being struck by a car while riding her bicycle in Cheektowaga is remembering her dedication to her family, her patients and her passion for cycling.Shari Kersch, 65, was riding her bicycle to Stiglmeier Park on the afternoon of Sunday, Oct. 25, when she was struck by a car at the intersection of Strasmer and Transit roads, according to her son, Jordan Kersch.She was taken to ECMC, where she died three days later."None of us could have ever imagined something as horrific as this happening," Jordan Kersch said.Shari Kersch was a mother of five who had spent 43 years working as a nurse, most recently as the director of nursing at Brothers of Mercy. She had retired just six months before the crash."She loved nursing. She loved helping people," her son said. "She's probably helped thousands of people throughout her entire life."In retirement, Kersch, who lived in Depew, spent more time doing something else she loved: riding her bicycle."She loved cycling, and she's very passionate about cycling," Jordan said.WATCH: 'She loved helping people': Family remembers nurse killed while riding bicycleHe said his mother was headed to Stiglmeier Park when the crash happened."She was immediately rushed to ECMC," Jordan said. "It was becoming very clear that she wasn't gonna get better, and we had to make a very difficult decision to let her go on Wednesday."Kersch's death has left her family facing not only grief, but major changes in their lives.Jordan said his mother had devoted significant time to caring for her wife, Margaret, who is recovering from a stroke.She was also deeply involved in the life of her son Jason, Jordan's twin brother, who is autistic and lives in a group home."She would go every single weekend, pick him up, take him out to eat, do all sorts of things with him," Jordan said. "She absolutely loves Jason."Jordan and Jason had celebrated their birthdays just one day before their mother was struck.As the family mourns, Jordan said he hopes people who knew his mother will share their memories of her."I love to hear stories about her if anybody ever wants to reach out to me and, you know, give me a memory of her," he said. local.body: The Town of Orchard Park is putting RV parking lot owners on notice for the 2027-28 year as it pauses the issue for now, but officials say safety requirements will continue to be enforced.The update follows concerns raised earlier this fall over RV parking on private property across from Highmark Stadium, where campers have gathered during Buffalo Bills home games.At the Oct. 7 Town Board meeting, Supervisor Joe Liberti said the town planned to pause the RV parking issue for now, with the matter expected to be addressed in the 2027-28 timeframe.In response to a follow-up inquiry, Liberti clarified that RV parking lot owners are being put on notice for 2027-28.WATCH: Orchard Park delays RV parking enforcement, keeps safety rules in placeHe also emphasized that the town is not suspending enforcement of safety-related requirements."We are still enforcing safety, egress, emergency access, sanitation," Liberti said.He added that permitted commercial lots must continue meeting site safety and inspection standards, which will remain in place for public safety.The town's latest position comes after RV owners raised concerns about enforcement of local parking regulations and the potential impact on a longstanding Bills game-day tradition.It remains unclear what specific changes, if any, the town may consider for RV parking in the 2027-28 time frame.

local.body: A panel of University at Buffalo political science experts says Tuesday's midterm election results are considered “seismic," as a "blue wave" swept through the U.S.Democrats won big — both locally and nationally — taking control of both the House and the Senate. But exit polls also showed voters were deeply concerned about corruption and democracy."People were pushing for greater transparency and for democratically held elections," said Conor Dowling, professor of Political Science at UB."But President Trump signaling accepted results, I think, is a big thing for democracy, and probably consistent with what maybe the Republican party was seeing in some of the exit polls," said Dowling.Neiheisel offered a more cautious take on how voters interpret those issues."As somebody who studies political extremism, I may be less hopeful that the electorate is seeing things like democracy and things like corruption in precisely the same way. local.title: Buffalo Guinea Pig Mafia Rescue over capacity after taking in more than 20 guinea pigs in three weeks
local.summary: The Williamsville-based rescue is seeking medical foster homes and donations to help care for more than 100 guinea pigs, including 13 recently rescued from Syracuse.
local.body: A Western New York animal rescue is asking for the community's help after taking in more than 20 guinea pigs in just three weeks, leaving the organization over capacity.The Buffalo Guinea Pig Mafia Rescue, based in Williamsville, currently cares for approximately 112 guinea pigs, according to Executive Director Jessica Meacham.Among the recent arrivals are 13 guinea pigs from Syracuse that came to the rescue severely malnourished and with fight wounds. Several required shaving and antiseptic medication, and all have needed additional medical care.Meacham said three of the females may also be pregnant.The influx has created additional challenges for the small organization, which typically houses 15 to 20 guinea pigs at its rescue center. Cages are now being placed on floors and tables, with some double-stacked to accommodate the growing population."It's been really tough for us because we're a small organization," Meacham said. "Taking in 20 at any one given time, especially 20 that have severe medical needs, is really hard."WATCH: Buffalo Guinea Pig Mafia Rescue over capacity after taking in more than 20 guinea pigs in three weeksHow the community can helpThe rescue's biggest immediate need is medical foster homes. Meacham said finding temporary homes for five or six guinea pigs would help ease overcrowding and allow the organization to return to its typical setup.The rescue provides foster families with cages, hay, pellets and vitamin C. Foster families are responsible for providing fresh vegetables and helping with the animals' daily care.The organization is also accepting donations of:HayUnscented paper beddingUnscented laundry detergentAll donated supplies must be new and unopened.The rescue typically goes through two to three bags of hay each day, making supply donations especially important.Those interested in fostering, donating or learning more can contact the Buffalo Guinea Pig Mafia Rescue through its Facebook page. The organization's Amazon wish list is can be found here. Meacham said the need for help continues to grow, but community support can make a difference in giving these guinea pigs the care and attention they need.

local.title: Buffalo voters approve all 11 proposed changes to city charter
local.summary: Buffalo voters approved all 11 proposed changes to the city charter on Election Day, giving the green light to a series of changes involving how city government operates.
local.body: Buffalo voters approved all 11 proposed changes to the city charter on Election Day, giving the green light to a series of changes involving how city government operates.The city charter essentially serves as the rule book for Buffalo city government. All 11 ballot measures passed Tuesday, with even the closest proposal approved by 33 percentage points.“I think it was great. I think people paid attention to it,” said Laurence Rubin, chair of the City of Buffalo Charter Revision Commission.The commission worked with members of the community to fine-tune the proposals before they were put before voters.The newly approved measures cover a range of issues, including clarifying mayoral succession, reviewing inactive city boards and creating new community-driven commissions.One of those is a new Civilian Police Advisory Commission, which is intended to provide more opportunities for the public to engage on issues involving community policing."More interaction, more communication, more opportunity for the public to be heard about their concerns," Rubin said. "And I think that at least our current administration seems to be interested in hearing that."WATCH: Buffalo voters approve all 11 proposed changes to city charterAnother approved measure amends the city charter to establish a Commission on Human Rights, focused on the protection and promotion of human rights for Buffalo residents."They can look at issues about how local government, city government, is dealing with issues of human rights, or impacting on human rights in the City of Buffalo," Rubin said. "But it actually has a broader mandate that it can go beyond that and look community-wide at issues about human rights."Rubin said many of the charter changes take effect immediately, while the process of creating the newly approved commissions is expected to take a couple of months.With voters approving all 11 measures, Buffalo will now begin implementing the charter changes. While many provisions can take effect immediately, Rubin said establishing the new commissions will require additional time.

entertainment.title: ‘Married at First Sight UK’ Canceled Amid Rape Claims, Review Finds “Implicit Pressure” on Contestants to Be Intimate
entertainment.summary: CEO Priya Dogra has decided that the "right course was to bring 'MAFS UK' on Channel 4 to an end."
entertainment.body:
Channel 4 has canceled Married at First Sight UK after two contestants claimed they had been raped during the filming of the show.

That decision was unveiled despite an external review giving the green light to produce future installments with improvements to the welfare framework. The suggestions for Channel 4 and production company CPL included installing CCTV, putting locks in shared bedrooms, and giving contestants access to a panic button.

“Whilst the review praised the welfare protocols in place and made no findings that Channel 4 breached the Ofcom Code or that the format is inherently unsafe, I have to consider when is the right time for Channel 4 to move on from a format,” said the broadcaster’s CEO Priya Dogra. “The recommendations are eminently sensible and feasible, but considering their wholesale implementation provoked fundamental questions about the editorial proposition of a show that, I believe, has now run its course over ten years.” Related Stories Movies 'Fruitcakes: Dawn of Drag' Goes Back to 'Happy Gays,' "Reclaiming History" Through a Timely Film (Exclusive Trailer and Chat) TV Sophie Stone Has Been Writing a Play and a Sitcom and Says, "There's So Much to Gain" From Our Differences

Earlier this year, a group of ex-participants came forward in a BBC Panorama investigation, where it came to light that two women on MAFS UK — where singletons are matched, by experts, with a stranger and meet for the first time at a mock wedding — alleged violent attacks.

The first said her husband had raped her and later threatened her with an acid attack, while a second woman told Channel 4 and CPL before broadcast about being allegedly raped by her husband. Her episodes, according to the BBC program, were still aired. A third woman, Shona Manderson, the only one to have revealed her identity, accused her onscreen husband of a non-consensual sex act. The men involved deny the claims, challenging the details of each woman’s account.

All of the former participants who spoke to the BBC said Channel 4 did not do enough to protect them. The BBC reported at the time that Channel 4 was aware of some allegations before broadcast, but had previously told Panorama that all of the claims were “wholly uncorroborated and disputed.” The broadcaster did, however, pull all episodes of the program from its streaming and linear services.

On Thursday, Channel 4 released the findings of an external review into the show, split into two parts: A review by law firm Clyde & Co, and a future-facing review by former Controller of BBC One, Lorraine Heggessey. Channel 4 stated at the top of the document that it is “not in a position to investigate or adjudicate on the […] allegations as those would be for the police and the courts to investigate and determine.”

entertainment.title: ‘Fruitcakes: Dawn of Drag’ Goes Back to ‘Happy Gays,’ “Reclaiming History” Through a Timely Film (Exclusive Trailer and Chat)
entertainment.summary: Finnish filmmaker Vesa Kuosmanen discusses his doc, premiering at Tallinn, how it feels like a story for our time amid a backlash against trans and queer rights, and how fear drives anger.
entertainment.body:
Happy Gays . That was the name of Finland’s first drag show in the late 1970s, which drew big, loud and proud audiences. Among the people on stage back then were Mummo, one of the first openly gay men in the country, and his best friend Jolanda. Now, you can relive, or experience for the first time, some of the excitement of those days in the new documentary Fruitcakes: Dawn of Drag , which will celebrate its world premiere during the 30th edition of the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival ( PÖFF ) in Estonia.

But it isn’t all about fun and panache. After all, not everyone was happy to hear about the now-legendary drag show and its performers’ joy back in the day. And when the AIDS crisis hit, fear and violence were among the responses. In 1988, Mummo was killed in his home in Helsinki. Related Stories TV Sophie Stone Has Been Writing a Play and a Sitcom and Says, "There's So Much to Gain" From Our Differences Movies 'Sounds of the Desert' Explores Lives, Music and Cosmic Visions of Two Members of the Sun Ra Arkestra (Exclusive Tallinn Trailer)

Finnish filmmaker Vesa Kuosmanen ( Just Animals ) has a view of that building from a window in his apartment. Amid the more recent backlash against queer rights, he started thinking about making a film about that not-so-distant past.

He met the aforementioned Jolanda, a retired archivist. More than 30 years after his friend’s death, Jolanda opened up his own archive for Fruitcakes: Dawn of Drag . And the filmmaker and Jolanda invited a new generation of drag artists to bring Happy Gays back to the stage. The heartwarming film takes us on a ride through archive and new footage and rehearsals and re-enactments of Happy Gays that bring up happy but also painful memories, along with a different side of the at times curmudgeonly Jolanda. And it puts a spotlight on drag’s power to bring people together, to celebrate and to endure discrimination.

Kuosmanen also wrote the film and edited it together with Jussi Sandhu, with cinematography courtesy of Mikko Kelloniemi. Rise and Shine has boarded the film and is handling world sales. “ Fruitcakes is much more than only a very entertaining trip down memory lane of drag culture in the 1980s,” says Rise and Shine’s Anja Dziersk. “It is a masterpiece of Finnish humor, connected to a very timely message as we see queer life being challenged and threatened every day.”
