Looking for People to Unfollow was announced as the 2026 AMP champ on Thursday (Nov. 11), beating out a nine-strong shortlist that included LPs by Genesis Owusu, Grace Cummings, Julia Jacklin and Karnivool, as decided by a music industry panel.

Based in Melbourne, Australia, and born in South Africa of Sri Lankan heritage, Ecca Vandal dropped her self-titled debut in 2017. With her long-percolating followup LP, plaudits came from Zane Lowe, and Spotify’s international editorial team, which anointed her as one of the streaming giant’s Artists To Watch 2026 . Australia’s Triple J locked-in Looking for People to Unfollow as its feature album of the week.

The AMP extends a breakout year for the genre-bending artist, during which she performed at Coachella, her first-ever performance at a major U.S. festival; made her U.S. TV debut with a performance on Jimmy Kimmel Live; and landed seven nominations for the 2026 ARIA Awards, to be presented later this month in Sydney.

Now, she’s on the final leg of her tour in support of Looking for People to Unfollow , with sold-out dates to come in Brisbane, Melbourne and Sydney.

Speaking to Billboard about how audiences should prepare for the live Ecca Vandal experience, she remarked: “Aside from the flashing lights, I’d say come as you are and be prepared to lose yourself for a little while. I’ll be bringing all my energy so bring yours too. I love when a show feels like a little world that only exists for us for that hour, with everyone just collectively losing it.”

Modeled on the U.K.’s Mercury Prize, the AMP launched in 2005 as a platform to “discover, reward and promote new Australian music of excellence,” and is today coveted as the most prestigious national award for the album format.

entertainment.title: Sony Pictures Q2 Profits Soars to $581 Million Due to ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’
entertainment.summary: Revenue topped $3.23 billion for the period in which the movie unit released 'Evil Dead Burn,' 'Insidious: Out of the Further' and 'Resident Evil.'
entertainment.body:
If you need more proof as to why Sony will never give up the rights to Spider-Man , just check out the studio’s latest quarterly results. Spider-Man: Brand New Day ‘s massive global box office success supercharged Sony Pictures Entertainment operating income for its fiscal second quarter (the three months ending September 30, 2026), with profits growing a whopping 525 percent to $581 million from the comparable period a year before. Q2 sales up a healthy 37 percent to $3.23 billion year-on-year.

SPE comprises the motion pictures division, television productions and media networks. Related Stories Lifestyle Jon Bernthal Adds Another Notch on Packed 2026 Résumé by Fronting Fear of God Campaign Movies Dwayne Johnson and Jack Black Get Flirty in 'Jumanji: Open World' Trailer

If we focus just on the motion pictures division (which includes movie sales from theatrical, home entertainment and television/streaming), Q2 revenue grew 155 percent y-o-y to $1.82 billion, fueled by Brand New Day , but also buoyed by the release of Evil Dead Burn (international rights only) , Insidious: Out of the Further and Resident Evil .

A more granular look at just theatrical revenue in Q2, SPE saw revenues jump 1,020 percent.

Looking ahead to the next quarter, things look less rosy for SPE, with The Social Reckoning and Klara and the Sun both already having bombed at the box office. Although the studio has high hopes on Jumanji: Open World which opens on Christmas Day.

The boffo earnings at the film unit, covered up big drops in revenue elsewhere. SPE’s TV unit saw Q2 revenue reach $483 million, a 31 percent fall from $701 million in the same period a year earlier. SPE’s major streaming television productions from the period included the latest seasons of Starz’s Outlander : Blood of My Blood , Netflix’s My Life with the Walter Boys and Apple TV’s Dark Matter and Star City. Broadcast staples Jeopardy! and Wheel of Fortune , and their various spinoffs, as well as ABC’s Shark Tank added to the TV unit’s revenues.

Elsewhere, Sony Music Entertainment expanded on its strong performance, with Q2 revenue climbing to $3.72 billion (¥592.3 billion, up 11.25 percent from ¥532.4 billion in the same period a year ago). Michael Jackson’s Thriller remained a top global seller as the halo from the biopic continued, helping the album to become Sony’s second best-selling project for the quarter behind ATEEZ’s GOLDEN HOUR: Part.5 .

entertainment.title: Sophie Stone Has Been Writing a Play and a Sitcom and Says, “There’s So Much to Gain” From Our Differences
entertainment.summary: The 'Falling' and 'Retreat' star discusses what it means to be part of the 2026 U.K. BAFTA Breakthrough cohort and how the world has "a collective chance to listen to what deaf people are saying."
entertainment.body:
Falling star Sophie Stone is one of the 21 rising creatives who are part of the 2026 U.K. BAFTA Breakthrough cohort , supported by Netflix.

The English actress plays Susan, the deaf sister of Catholic priest David, portrayed by Paapa Essiedu, whose forbidden love with devoted nun Anna, played by Keeley Hawes , in the romantic drama.

The deaf Stone has also seen her profile rise with her role in fellow BAFTA Breakthrough talent Ted Evans’ feature Retreat and revenge thriller series Reunion . Related Stories Movies 'Sounds of the Desert' Explores Lives, Music and Cosmic Visions of Two Members of the Sun Ra Arkestra (Exclusive Tallinn Trailer) Movies Milcho Manchevski's 'Sister Brother Manhole Cover' Wins Top Prize at Tokyo Film Fest

In an email Q&A, Stone shared her reaction to being part of the new BAFTA Breakthrough cohort and her career so far and ahead.

How exciting is it to be selected as a BAFTA Breakthrough creative, and what do you hope to get out of the experience? BAFTA has always been known as a nurturing and celebratory body that recognizes varying roles in the industry and their skillset; I’ve always admired the people that pass through this [program], whether early on or later in their careers. It has meant that there’s the rare potential to meet creatives I’ve admired and watched climb the ranks, earning respect and creating beautiful work. It’ll mean an element of equity and fruitful connections for someone who often isn’t considered in rooms where networking and creative discussions can take place, elevating ideas and dreams into existence.

I am so excited for all the possibilities this might bring and a reminder that it isn’t too late for me. There’s so much more to discover and this playground is a huge honor to be let into. I hope to meet some heroes and branch into new fields of gold to build exciting projects. You were picked as a BAFTA Breakthrough talent for your role in Falling, but also turned heads before that in Retreat . How much did the latter appeal to you? Ted Evans had been writing [it] with me in mind for Mia for 10 years. We did a short film version where my role was very different – a questioning follower within a cult – to then becoming the leader of a cult in the feature. We built her around our knowledge of both deaf and isolated communities, making her someone you wanted to trust and feel safe with yet question what we deem as acts of love, for the greater good.

entertainment.title: ‘Black Doves’ Season 2 Review: Keira Knightley and Ben Whishaw Return for More Crackling Chemistry and Bittersweet Thrills in Netflix Spy Thriller
entertainment.summary: Neve Campbell and Ambika Mod join the sophomore outing of Joe Barton's drama following an undercover agent and an assassin who work for a private intelligence agency in London.
entertainment.body:
En route to a murderous mission, trunk loaded with what must be a small platoon’s worth of machine guns and hand grenades, four deadly operatives suddenly find themselves mired in a heated battle … over who gets to control the playlist.

Zoomer assassins Williams (Ella Lily Hyland) and Eleanor (Gabrielle Creevy) like to hype themselves up to raucous party music ( “Picture this, I’m a bag of dicks” ). Triggerman Sam ( Ben Whishaw ) prefers the more downbeat vibe of a low voice over a slow piano. Undercover agent Helen ( Keira Knightley ), not much of a music nerd, suggests mainstream stuff — Olly Murs, maybe, or early Beatles. Related Stories Movies BAFTA Breakthrough Ted Evans Shares What Sign Language Taught Him About Film - and What's Next After 'Retreat' Movies 'The Incomer' Attracted Domhnall Gleeson and Moby and Got Its Creator on the BAFTA Breakthrough List. Now, He's Working on a Plan B Film. Black Doves The Bottom Line Sometimes funny, sometimes sad, always charming. Airdate: Thursday, Nov. 5 (Netflix) Cast: Ben Whishaw, Keira Knightley, Sarah Lancashire, Gabrielle Creevy, Ella Lily Hyland, Ambika Mod, Andrew Buchan, Sylvia Hoeks, Neve Campbell Creator: Joe Barton

The pleasure of Black Doves is that somehow, all these picks seem entirely apropos for the mood concocted by creator Joe Barton , equal parts irreverent and melancholic and broadly crowd-pleasing. In combination with a top-notch cast, witty dialogue and solid action, that tone is the show’s not-so-secret weapon — the thing that allows it to glide over any narrative pitfalls it might hit along the way, if not always to avert them completely.

Like so many critically acclaimed streaming shows, the spy thriller is returning for its six-hour second season after enough time away ( nearly two years ) that you’d be forgiven for forgetting Sam and Helen had any outstanding business at all. Unlike a lot of its brethren — but helpfully for fans like yours truly who remember enjoying the series, but not necessary what transpired within it — it’s not a show that requires much recall of anything but the bare basics of the plot.

Which, in case your memory is really spotty, are these: The title refers to a private intelligence operation, based in London but loyal to no particular country. Clever Helen is one of its prize jewels, having honeypotted her way into a marriage and two kids with a politician (Andrew Buchan’s Wallace) who, as of season two, has just ascended to the office of prime minister. Lonely Sam is her best friend and literal partner in crime, and although the unpredictable nature of their professional field means they regularly go long stretches without contact, each is always there for the other when they call.

“Done the way that Big AI is proposing,” ARIA CEO Annabelle Herd remarked in October , “it would devastate the music industry and make Australia a pariah for rights holders globally.”

The International Confederation of Music Publishers (ICMP) agrees with the assessment .

Earlier in 2026, APRA AMCOS hosted the CISAC board of directors in Sydney. AI was at the top of the agenda . Billboard recently caught up with Phelan for an update on an issue whose “implications are global.”

Billboard: Just how concerned should the international music community be, and why should the situation in Australia — of all places — deserve our attention?

John Phelan : What’s on the table is a plan, cooked as much in Silicon Valley as Sydney, to enable tech and AI companies to utilize the world’s digital music for ingestion and training.

The downstream GenAI product would be paid for. But the proposal is still as commercially and legally harmful as could be. entertainment.title: The $1.4 Billion ‘No-Brainer’ Opportunity The Music Industry Is Missing
entertainment.summary: Soundtrack, the music streamer used by restaurants and retailers globally, estimates billions are lost in revenue every year in the U.S. from businesses that unwittingly stream music illegally.
entertainment.body:
That’s according to a new study released Thursday (Nov. 5) by Soundtrack, a commercial music streaming platform backed by Spotify that is now used by 60,000 businesses in 75 countries. Related Kenny MacPherson, Veteran Music Publisher and Big Deal Music Co-Founder, Dies at 71 Jessica Lynch

The independent study, which Soundtrack commissioned, surveyed around 1,500 representatives of some 15,000 U.S. business locations and found that only 19% of those that play music are fully compliant with commercial music requirements. Nearly 80% of U.S. businesses use consumer streaming services, which are only licensed for personal use, to play music in-store, and just 5% reported having licenses from all four major performing rights organizations (PROs): ASCAP, BMI, GMR and SESAC.

At a time when the revenue growth from subscription and ad-supported streaming is slowing, Sars says the music industry could “unlock exponential growth” in the money it collects from U.S. businesses by turning their attention to this “extreme” level of non-compliance.

“People are playing music already, but they simply don’t know that it’s not licensed for commercial use. They haven’t read the terms and no one has told them,” Sars tells Billboard. “It is what you guys in the U.S. would call a pretty big no-brainer. If you’re playing music in your business, artists should be fairly compensated. There is a rate structure in place, and you can’t use a personal service in your business. But it’s complicated.”

Commercial music streaming in businesses can be the next growth area in music, Sars says. Soundtrack says it recently partnered with SESAC to round out its pitch to U.S. businesses.

Based in Sweden, Soundtrack generates roughly 60 million euros ($67 million) in annual recurring revenue and is on track to generate $100 million by 2028. Previously called Soundtrack Your Brand, the company raised $15 million in 2023 from investors like Matt Pincus’ MUSIC and Dundee Partners, who joined existing investors Balderton Capital, Fuel Venture Capital, Industrifonden, Telia, DIG and Matt Spetzler.

“Ultimately, our aim is to create a healthy ecosystem for the background music industry by growing the ‘pie’ for music creators and rights-holders, while not breaking the bank for hard-working businesses,” SARS says.

entertainment.title: The Top 26 Looks in 2026 (So Far), According to 50 of Hollywood’s Biggest Stylists
entertainment.summary: The Hollywood Reporter presents its inaugural data-driven stylists’ survey, in which tastemakers voted on their peers’ most impressive looks this year. What’s being served: fashion as art.
entertainment.body:
In the three decades since red carpets have become synonymous with Hollywood couture, celebrity stylists have outpaced fashion editors, models, moguls and, more recently, content creators as the true arbiters of the town’s taste. No one else has the number of media impressions that top Hollywood stylists do, with many of them pulling in millions of followers. Of course, Beyoncé, Rihanna and Taylor Swift have 500 million-plus Instagram fans each, but much of the engagement is driven by what their stylists are putting on their backs.

That’s why, as this year winds down, THR reached out to the many pros who’ve now achieved fame in their own right for dressing the most visible personages in the world. What did we learn? The newish Parisian design duo behind Matières Fécales — Hannah Rose Dalton and Steven Raj Bhaskaran — have captured stylists’ hearts the most, while Matthieu Blazy’s Chanel, Jonathan Anderson’s Dior and Anthony Vaccarello’s Saint Laurent also number among Hollywood’s favorite designers. Feathers still are flying on red carpet fits for all genders. The sheer look continues to show off, but cutouts and two-piece looks are taking over the body-part wars. Lace, lingerie and leather are now completely red carpet-worthy. Slinky close fits and strong tailoring are forever. And so, apparently, is fashion’s idolization of Zendaya. We could have easily included three or more of her looks, but to keep the list varied and fun, we chose only one top fit per actor or actress. The methodology behind the list included tabulating the top 10 looks chosen by 50-plus stylists, prioritizing by the number of votes each look received, and then, to break ties, bringing in rankings. The result: a realistic look at coming trends and which designers and designs rank the highest for Hollywood, by the world’s top tastemakers.

At the NYC premiere of The Odyssey on July 14, America’s favorite zillennial stunned in Matières Fécales’ “Ange” gown. Styled by Law Roach, the micro-hand-pleated chiffon creation sported white rooster feather wings designed to evoke Zendaya’s character in the movie: Greek goddess Athena. “What I loved most about the Matières angel look,” says stylist Ilaria Urbinati (her clients: Dwayne Johnson, Barry Keoghan) “is how cohesively ethereal it felt from head to toe. It didn’t look costume-y. She looked like a painting. Not many could pull it off.” Adds stylist Tara Swennen (Kristen Stewart, Ali Wong), “It literally took my breath away.”

entertainment.title: Six Hollywood Consequences of Tuesday’s Democratic Blockbuster
entertainment.summary: From the federal tax credit to cable-news trolling to AI regulation, the world looks a lot different today than just days before the election.
entertainment.body:
The massive showing by Democrats in Tuesday’s midterm elections enmeshes in the lives of all Americans. But the entertainment industry has a particular role to play, given its charge to tell stories — to explain America to itself.

And now, suddenly, there’s a whole new chapter to write. But man, that sounds awfully high-minded. There are far more concrete examples of how politics will change the entertainment industry. Here are six realms that could look a lot different after Tuesday’s domination. Bring on the film money? The federal film tax credit has had a little bit of momentum with both Republican lawmakers like Tim Scott, Brian Jack and Nathaniel Moran and Democrats such as Adam Schiff, Laura Friedman and Linda Sanchez, all of whom introduced a bill last month to establish the 20% credit for certain labor costs. Where does Tuesday leave it? Well, the good news is all the lead champions in Congress have won re- election and will be back to work next session (though Scott may have to spend a few extra minutes in the morning wiping egg off his face for his “unequivocal” assertion that Republicans would maintain Senate control). The question is whether they can rally enough fellow lawmakers behind it. On paper, Republicans would want to join the cause, as it’s a win for them at a time when those won’t come easy. Doubly so for President Donald Trump, who will be eager to crow about…something, and bringing some jobs back to the U.S. allows for the chirp. The snag is that the tax credit reduces the U.S. tax base at a time of both a massive deficit and when many Democrats are promising a restoration of benefits — i.e., the kinds of things you need a deep tax base for. Supporters will argue that this is tax revenue that wouldn’t have happened anyway if productions are shipping overseas (sometimes but not always true) and that it will benefit workers (yes, it will trickle down, but the actual rebate goes to producers, not all of whom need the cash). On paper this should still stand a decent shot. But Congressional turnovers can mess with priorities. Put this in the unknown column. Texas artists saw it all along No one around the cable-news dial could quite believe that Texas had elected a Democratic senator for the first time in 38 years or governor for the first time in 32. Harry Enten was so in disbelief he almost got into a fight with his accent. We should have paid closer attention to creatives. They’ve been telling us how it’s possible — telling us of another Texas — all along. Natalie Maines of The (then-Dixie) Chicks famously and at the expense of her career told a London audience at the start of the Iraq War in 2003 that “we do not want this war, this violence. And we’re ashamed that the president of the United States is from Texas.” But the idea has been creeping into plenty of other Texans’ work too — in the films of Richard Linklater and his anti-exploitation 2006 movie Fast Food Nation and the arched-eyebrow-to-false-jingoism Last Flag Flying in 2017. Or Mike Judge, pushing back against George W. Bush-era compliance in 2006’s retroactive documentary Idiocracy. Or even just the work of an Austinite like David Modigliani and his 2019 nonfiction piece Running with Beto . (Actually, Beto walked so James Talarico could run.) We haven’t always paid attention. No doubt we’ll soon start hearing other artists around the country tell us a place is a lot more Democratic than its Republican politicians want to project. After Tuesday, it’s worth listening to them. Anti-media trolling You know how you’re going for some minor medical procedure and the doctor’s like, “In the short term, it will hurt like hell, but then you’ll feel a lot better?” I suspect we’ll get a whole lash-out at mainstream media figures by Trump and members of his administration after Tuesday’s drubbing. “Outlets are failing,” “hosts should be fired,” you know the lyrics. But lame ducks tend to get lamer as their term wears on, and I suspect once Trump sees how little effect this is having — the meager few days of Jimmy Kimmel suspension’s after the Charlie Kirk joke last year will practically look like a Colbert canning by comparison — we’ll start seeing these instances fade as his attention turns elsewhere. Spasms from the FCC are still possible, Brendan Carr writing letters to this media company or that asking them to drop by for a not-so-friendly visit. But how hard do you want to go on these when — oh yes, you’re not a presidential cabinet department but an agency overseen and funded by….Congress? The Carr witch hunts and saber rattles of the past two years are going to get a lot quieter. Who knows? Maybe the media companies will stop quaking in their boots and even restore a DEI program or two. David Ellison ’s true colors For months we’ve been told by Ellison apologists — and David Ellison — that the new owner of Warner Bros. wasn’t actually a Trumper; he just played one at UFC fights. Ellison needed Trump to get his deals through, so it was all realpolitik . Well, now he doesn’t need that — in fact, if anything, a Trump association hurts him with a new Congress. So does he reveal himself to be the pragmatist his defenders say (or even the liberal on many issues that he says he is)? Or, with his Trump cover falling away, does he just unmask as the conservative he’s been all along? First test: Alex Gibney’s Musk documentary, coming in a few months on HBO. Does Ellison still release it despite its targeting of the leading GOP donor? Musk just paid a lot of money to Skydance, potentially so HBO doesn’t air it, though he has bigger challenges to worry about right now . entertainment.title: Judge Torn on Lil Durk Bail Question After Murder-for-Hire Verdict: ‘A Question of Psychology’
entertainment.summary: The rapper's lawyers want him out of jail ahead of a second racketeering trial. Prosecutors say he'll flee.
entertainment.body:
A judge is struggling with whether to let out Lil Durk on bail following his acquittal on murder-for-hire charges but before a second racketeering trial.

The “All My Life” hitmaker (Durk Banks) was found not guilty in September of taking out a hit on rival rapper Quando Rondo . Durk’s lawyers are now pushing for his release after more than two years in jail, offering to put up all his future music royalties as bond and even getting letters of support from Jay-Z and J. Cole .

Judge Michael W. Fitzgerald weighed the request during a Wednesday (Nov. 4) court hearing, attended by Billboard . The judge was torn, given that Durk attempted to flee to Dubai before his original 2024 arrest and still faces another trial next summer for allegedly operating his Only the Family (OTF) label as a violent gang.

On the one hand, Judge Fitzgerald said “not that much has changed” for Durk and that “even an innocent person would be tempted to flee” at this point. On the other, however, he noted that Durk “has a very strong incentive now to let the legal system play out, so the acquittals really do change the calculation a great deal.”

“It’s a question of psychology,” said the judge. “Would he flee?”

Durk’s team says the answer is no. His attorney Drew Findling argued Wednesday that the rapper “understands how the system works” and wants a second jury to find him not guilty again. Fellow defense lawyer Christy O’Connor also pointed out that the proposed bond package truly encompasses all his future earnings on his music, so he would be left destitute if he went on the lam.

Prosecutors want Durk to stay in jail. Assistant U.S. Attorney Daniel Weiner said Durk has “absolutely no respect for authority” and would “run amok” if let out. Weiner also pointed out that Durk could simply flee to a non-extradition country and make new music. “He could accumulate more wealth,” said the prosecutor.

Judge Fitzgerald ultimately took the bail motion under submission and will issue a written ruling in due course.
